{id:"cure", name:"Curative", html:`
<div class="card">
  <h3>Resection</h3>
  <p class="kicker"><span class="pill p-std">Standard</span> <span class="grade A">A</span> <span class="flag">EXPERTISE</span>   Localised HCC with technically complete resection, adequate future remnant, preserved function and acceptable portal-hypertension risk.</p>
  <p>In selected multifocal or larger tumours, resectability is determined by expert hepatobiliary review rather than size alone. After resection, obtain multiphase liver imaging and chest imaging every 3–6 months and continue long-term surveillance, because recurrence risk persists indefinitely.</p>
  <div class="callout"><b>AASLD advises against routine neoadjuvant or adjuvant systemic therapy for resection or local ablation; use clinical trials.</b> The updated IMbrave050 analysis lost the recurrence-free survival signal seen at the first interim analysis (HR 0.90, 95% CI 0.72–1.12), with overall survival immature and numerically unfavourable (HR 1.26). {{37871608|41580093|39992051}}</div>
</div>
<div class="card">
  <h3>Establishing clinically significant portal hypertension</h3>
  <p class="kicker">Child-Pugh class, MELD and the absence of decompensation establish preserved hepatic function. They do not establish portal pressure.</p>
  <p>BCLC treats the two as separate axes. A patient can be Child-Pugh A with a normal MELD and still have CSPH — this is the most common way the resection decision is made on incomplete information. CSPH is an HVPG ≥10 mmHg. BCLC accepts surrogate markers, cites Baveno VII for them and keeps HVPG as the gold standard; the table below applies the later Baveno VIII statements. {{41151697|42624290|35120736}}</p>
  <details class="more" open><summary>The Baveno criteria, in full</summary><div class="moreinner">
  <div class="tablewrap"><table><thead><tr><th style="width:18%">Criterion</th><th style="width:38%">Finding</th><th>Interpretation</th></tr></thead><tbody>
   <tr><td><b>Reference standard</b></td><td>HVPG ≥10 mmHg.</td><td>Defines CSPH. BCLC states HVPG remains the gold standard; non-invasive tools may rule it in or out. Measure it when the decision turns on it.</td></tr>
   <tr><td><b>Specific signs</b></td><td>Oesophageal or gastric varices; spontaneous portosystemic collaterals.</td><td>Baveno VIII identifies varices and portosystemic collaterals as generally indicating CSPH (statement 3.2d), with the exceptions below. The PSVD diagnostic score is a separate assessment; its spleen-stiffness >40 kPa item must not be used to rule in cirrhotic CSPH.</td></tr>
   <tr><td><b>Non-specific</b></td><td>Platelets <150 × 10⁹/L; splenomegaly.</td><td>Supportive findings do not establish CSPH alone. Ascites requires evaluation for hepatic decompensation and its cause. Absence of these findings does not exclude CSPH.</td></tr>
   <tr><td><b>Non-invasive rule-in</b></td><td>Liver stiffness ≥25 kPa, except in obese (BMI ≥30 kg/m²) MASLD; spleen stiffness (100 Hz) >55 kPa; ANTICIPATE or ANTICIPATE-NASH ≥75%; NICER ≥75%.</td><td>Baveno VIII statement 1.16 criteria for CSPH in compensated advanced chronic liver disease. In BCLC 0–A HCC without a >5 cm right-lobe nodule, ANTICIPATE or ANTICIPATE-NASH ≥75% is rated only as <b>highly suggestive</b> (statement 1.23, weak recommendation). Useful where HVPG is unavailable or declined — measure HVPG when the resection decision turns on it. <span class="flag">EXPERTISE</span></td></tr>
   <tr><td><b>What to record</b></td><td>The criterion used, its value, and the date.</td><td>“No portal hypertension” without a stated basis is not an acceptable entry when resection is being proposed.</td></tr>
  </tbody></table></div>
  </div></details>
  <details class="more"><summary>Three situations where a portosystemic shunt does not settle the question</summary><div class="moreinner">
  <p style="margin-top:4px"><i>Cured or controlled aetiology</i> — Baveno VIII states varices and collaterals may persist despite resolution of CSPH where the aetiology has been cured or controlled, and after recompensation they are not reliable indicators; in suppressed hepatitis B, cured hepatitis C or sustained alcohol abstinence a shunt alone does not establish current CSPH, so measure. <i>Portosinusoidal vascular disorder</i> — Baveno VII directs that when signs of portal hypertension are present with HVPG <10 mmHg, PSVD must be ruled out; the same imaging finding then carries a different diagnosis and a different operative risk. <i>Steatotic liver disease</i> — BCLC notes HVPG reliability may be suboptimal here, and signs of portal hypertension can occur with HVPG <10 mmHg in a minority of MASH cirrhosis; a sub-threshold measurement should not override a specific sign.</p>
  </div></details>
  <div class="callout amber" style="margin-top:14px"><b>Unresolved locally.</b> Whether a large spontaneous shunt can decompress the portal system enough to lower measured HVPG is a physiological concern raised in practice that this roadmap has not verified against a primary source. Hepatology should rule on it before a sub-10 value is treated as reassuring.</div>
</div>
<div class="card">
  <h3>Does CSPH bar resection? The randomised evidence cuts both ways</h3>
  <p>Portal pressure has been prognostic for post-resection decompensation since Bruix 1996. {{8831597}} A meta-analysis of 11 studies quantified it: CSPH assessed by any method raised 3-year post-resection mortality (pooled OR 2.09, 95% CI 1.52–2.88), 5-year mortality (OR 2.07, 95% CI 1.51–2.84) and early clinical decompensation (OR 3.04, 95% CI 2.02–4.59). {{25212123}} A hierarchical analysis of decompensation predictors reached the same conclusion. {{27248425}} BCLC's position is that with CSPH resection poses significant risk and transplantation offers better survival.</p>
  <p>The first multicentre randomised test compared partial hepatectomy with ablation, with or without TACE, in HBV-related HCC within Milan criteria and with CSPH (n = 80 per arm). Five-year overall survival was 69.5% with resection versus 64.9% (P = 0.325) and recurrence-free survival 46.2% versus 45.0% (P = 0.783) — no significant difference, in a trial too small to establish equivalence. Total complications were higher after resection (67.5% versus 20%, P < 0.001) but the excess was mainly Clavien-Dindo grade I; grade III–V complications occurred in 8/80 (10%) versus 2/80 (2.5%), with limited power for this comparison. Patients at high risk of postoperative failure were deliberately excluded. These data support selected discussion, not a general claim that resection is safe whenever CSPH is present. {{39322951}}</p>
  <div class="callout teal"><b>The roadmap adopts neither reading by default.</b> CSPH raises operative risk and should trigger transplant assessment in any patient within Milan criteria, but it is not an automatic bar where the remnant is adequate, the resection is minor or laparoscopic, and the hepatologist concurs. <b>Record which reading the board applied.</b> <span class="flag">EXPERTISE</span> <span class="flag">TX-TIMING</span></div>
</div>
<div class="card">
  <h3>Thermal ablation</h3>
  <p class="kicker"><span class="pill p-std">Standard</span> <span class="grade A">A</span>   Tumours ≤3 cm, up to three nodules, when a circumferential ablative margin can be achieved safely.</p>
  <p><b>Microwave versus radiofrequency.</b> MWA and RFA are both options. Sugimoto 2025 found lower two-year lesion-level local progression with MWA than single-needle RFA (20/122, 16.4%, versus 38/125, 30.4%; RR 0.54, 95% CI 0.33–0.87; P=.007), without a demonstrated overall-survival advantage. Most lesions were small; this does not establish superiority over every RFA system or a specific 3–4 cm subgroup. The earlier Vietti Violi superiority trial did not show a significant local-progression difference and did not test equivalence. {{29503247|39802807}}</p>
  <p><b>Resection versus ablation for small HCC.</b> The randomised SURF trial (308 registered, 301 analysed — 150 resection, 151 ablation; tumours ≤3 cm, up to three nodules, Child-Pugh ≤7) did not demonstrate superior recurrence-free survival for resection, but non-inferiority was not formally established and the trial was underpowered. The evidence supports the conclusion that for this phenotype the two are reasonable alternatives selected on anatomy, reserve and access — not that they are proven equivalent. {{35949295}}</p>
  <p>Use adjunctive technique or another modality for lesions abutting central bile ducts, bowel, gallbladder, diaphragm, heart or major vessels where a heat sink is expected. For tumours of 3–5 cm, single-probe thermal ablation alone should not be presented as curative-intent therapy.</p>
</div>`},

{id:"tx", name:"Transplant & allocation", html:`
<div class="card">
  <h3>Four kinds of statement, which the roadmap must not blur</h3>
  <dl class="kv">
   <dt>OPTN policy</dt><dd>Binding, and changes without notice to this document. Every numeric criterion must be re-verified against the current Policy 9 text before it is applied to a listing decision. {{OPTN9}}</dd>
   <dt>OPTN guidance</dt><dd>Nonbinding. Informs but does not compel the review board.</dd>
   <dt>Published evidence</dt><dd>MERITS-LT and XXL support downstaging as a strategy, but were generated under earlier allocation rules. {{34331914|32615109}}</dd>
   <dt>Local policy</dt><dd>May be stricter than OPTN policy and is the operative constraint at this centre. Where these conflict, the stricter of OPTN and local policy governs.</dd>
  </dl>
</div>
<div class="card">
  <h3>Eligibility pathways</h3>
  <div class="tablewrap"><table><thead><tr><th style="width:20%">Pathway</th><th>Criteria and action</th><th style="width:16%">Source type</th></tr></thead><tbody>
   <tr><td><b>Milan clinical criteria and OPTN T2 exception criteria</b></td><td>One lesion ≥2 cm and ≤5 cm, or 2–3 lesions each ≥1 cm and ≤3 cm; no macrovascular invasion; no extrahepatic spread. <b>The ≥2 cm and ≥1 cm lower limits are OPTN T2 rules</b> — Milan (Mazzaferro 1996) set upper limits only and excluded any vascular or lymph-node invasion. Lesions must meet OPTN class 5 imaging criteria. A solitary lesion <2 cm is T1 and does not attract exception points. Exception points accrue after the required waiting period and are capped relative to the median MELD at transplant in the acquisition circle.</td><td class="small">OPTN policy — verify current text</td></tr>
   <tr><td><b>Downstaging pool</b><br><span class="small muted">UNOS-DS</span></td><td>One lesion >5 cm and ≤8 cm; or 2–3 lesions each ≤5 cm with at least one lesion >3 cm and total diameter ≤8 cm; or 4–5 lesions each <3 cm with total diameter ≤8 cm. No macrovascular invasion or extrahepatic spread. Viable disease must be downstaged to within Milan and remain there for the required observation period. <b>v0.2 omitted the “at least one lesion >3 cm” qualifier in the 2–3 lesion group, which would have incorrectly routed T2 disease into the downstaging pool.</b></td><td class="small">OPTN policy — verify current text</td></tr>
   <tr><td><b>AFP rule</b></td><td>An AFP above 1,000 ng/mL blocks the standard exception until it falls below 500 ng/mL following locoregional therapy. A rise to 500 ng/mL or above at any later point requires review-board referral rather than automatic continuation. Record every AFP value with its date and the intervening treatment.</td><td class="small">OPTN policy — verify current text</td></tr>
   <tr><td><b>Macrovascular invasion or extrahepatic spread</b></td><td>Excludes the standardized HCC exception. NLRB guidance permits consideration of selected treated primary portal-vein branch invasion or ruptured HCC after at least 12 months of stability; main portal-vein or hepatic-vein invasion remains a contraindication. See the <a href="../transplant/hcc/">transplant assessment pathway</a> for the separate nonstandard review.</td><td class="small">OPTN policy</td></tr>
   <tr><td><b>Beyond the downstaging pool</b><br><span class="small muted">“all-comers”</span></td><td>Not an automatic exception route and not a recognised standard. Consider only for selected patients through transplant governance and the national liver review board, or within a clinical protocol, using sustained response and tumour biology rather than anatomy alone. Outcomes must be tracked prospectively.</td><td class="small">Local policy + registry</td></tr>
   <tr><td><b>Checkpoint exposure before transplant</b></td><td>Does not categorically exclude transplant, but the rejection risk and the required washout interval are unresolved; reported allograft rejection after pre-transplant checkpoint exposure is substantial and has been fatal. Require transplant-specific multidisciplinary review and a documented washout and immunosuppression plan agreed <b>before</b> the first dose, not after. Do not use checkpoint inhibitors as a casual bridging strategy. <span class="flag">TX-TIMING</span></td><td class="small">Evidence (low) + local policy</td></tr>
   <tr><td><b>Post-transplant checkpoint blockade</b></td><td><span class="pill p-avoid">Avoid</span> outside exceptional governance review. Pooled series report graft rejection in a substantial minority with appreciable graft loss and mortality. {{36102312}}</td><td class="small">Evidence (low)</td></tr>
  </tbody></table></div>
  <p style="margin-top:12px"><b>Refer early</b> — when within Milan criteria, when the downstaging pool may apply, or when recurrent HCC combined with the severity of the underlying liver disease makes resection or ablation a poor long-term solution. Repeated locoregional procedures while transplant referral is pending can delay assessment and reduce liver reserve. Refer early.</p>
</div>
<div class="card">
  <h3>Listing and allocation — calculated MELD initially, then MMaT-3</h3>
  <p class="kicker">OPTN Policy 9.5.I, full PDF pp. 196–199; guidance pp. 3–4, 7. Policy 9.4.C–E, full PDF pp. 188–189. Official policy checked 1 October 2026.</p>
  <dl class="kv">
   <dt>Authority</dt><dd>Policy 9.5 defines standardized exceptions; the Adult MELD Exceptions for Transplant Oncology document is review-board guidance, not policy and not a clinical standard of care. HCC and perihilar cholangiocarcinoma have standardized routes. Clinical candidacy and local protocol approval remain separate from allocation eligibility.</dd>
   <dt>MMaT</dt><dd>Median MELD at transplant for the donor hospital used in the match run — not one fixed national score. Under Policy 9.4.E an MMaT-relative exception below 15 is assigned 15. Exceptions generally require 90-day extensions (9.4.C).</dd>
   <dt>Route and score</dt><dd>Initial request and first extension receive calculated MELD; any extension after the first receives MMaT-3 (Table 9-10). Because each exception is valid for 90 days (Policy 9.4.A), two consecutive periods at calculated MELD elapse before MMaT-3 applies — approximately six months. <b>Policy states the score table, not a six-month rule.</b> Do not represent successful downstaging or referral as immediate exception points. The scores apply to candidates at least 18 years old at registration; Table 9-10 assigns a different score to a candidate registered between 12 and 18.</dd>
   <dt>Initial eligibility</dt><dd>Before locoregional treatment document lesion number and size on CT or MRI, qualifying Class 5 imaging or biopsy, initial chest CT, absence of extrahepatic spread and macrovascular invasion, nonresectability, AFP, and previous treatment. Standard T2 is one lesion 2–5 cm inclusive, or two to three lesions each 1–3 cm inclusive, with AFP ≤1000 ng/mL. Policy inclusive bounds govern; stricter inequalities in guidance examples do not replace them.</dd>
   <dt>Extensions</dt><dd>Every extension documents CT/MRI stage, treatment if tumour number fell, and AFP. Policy 9.5.I.i item 3 (full PDF p. 196) requires a chest CT only before an <b>initial</b> exception request and states it is not required for extensions; clinically indicated thoracic surveillance is a separate plan.</dd>
   <dt>Beyond-entry</dt><dd>Requires nonstandard review: T2 response, no extrahepatic disease, no macrovascular invasion, no AFP >1000, imaging at least four weeks after the last downstaging treatment, and six months from the first exception request.</dd>
   <dt>After transplant</dt><dd>Submit explant pathology within 60 days as required by Policy 9.5.I. Record graft outcome, recurrence surveillance and the accountable clinical team.</dd>
  </dl>
</div>`},

{id:"loco", name:"Locoregional", html:`
<div class="card">
  <h3>Decision sequence</h3>
  <div class="callout" style="margin-bottom:12px"><b>Do not use a universal ablation → SBRT → Y-90 → TACE → HAI → histotripsy sequence.</b> An upfront alternative chosen because of anatomy or organ reserve is not a post-progression second line.</div>
  <p>Compare resection, local ablation and transplant where appropriate at multidisciplinary review. Record the intended outcome, why alternatives fit or do not fit, the systemic-treatment plan, the reassessment date and the next action. After progression or toxicity, restage and reconsider complete treatment rather than automatically repeating the same procedure. <b>Device availability and specialty preference are not indications.</b></p>
  <p>Evidence differs by indication: radiation segmentectomy and ablative SBRT may be definitive treatments in localized HCC, while broader arterial therapy usually seeks control or conversion. Do not generalize findings from advanced-disease systemic-combination trials to small-tumour definitive therapy.</p>
</div>
<div class="tablewrap">
  <table><thead><tr><th style="width:13%">Modality</th><th style="width:10%">Label</th><th style="width:19%">Preferred phenotype</th><th style="width:19%">Caution or avoid</th><th>Comparative evidence and what governs selection</th></tr></thead><tbody id="locoBody"></tbody></table>
</div>
<div class="card">
  <h3>Stop and switch rules</h3>
  <p>After each locoregional treatment, reassess liver function, clinical recovery, AFP trajectory, new disease, and whether a viable target remains — not simply whether another procedure is technically possible.</p>
  <p><b>Switch away</b> from repeated TACE or broad embolisation for new decompensation, worsening ALBI or Child-Pugh, inability to achieve selective access, progression outside the treated territory, new macrovascular or extrahepatic progression, or inadequate response despite technically adequate treatment, assessed after each session. After one or two consecutive treatments without response, consider alternatives in MDT; document any reason to continue a curative or downstaging strategy.</p>
  <p><b>For radiation-based therapy, allow the expected delayed response pattern.</b> Apply the LI-RADS treatment response radiation algorithm and do not declare failure from persistent enhancement alone when the lesion is categorised as nonprogressing. Using the nonradiation algorithm after radioembolisation or SBRT is a recurring and consequential error. {{LIRADS}}</p>
  <p>Every repeat cycle must name, in the note: the viable target, the expected benefit, the liver-function cost, the owner, and the reassessment date.</p>
</div>
<div class="card">
  <h3>Portal-vein tumour thrombus</h3>
  <p>Systemic therapy is the default backbone <span class="grade A">A</span>. Adding radioembolisation or external beam radiotherapy is a <span class="pill p-reas">Reasonable</span> consideration <span class="grade B">B</span> when the anatomy is liver-confined, reserve is preserved, dosimetry is feasible, and there is a symptom-control, local-control or protocol-driven goal.</p>
  <p>The supporting randomised data for combined radiotherapy here come from a small single-centre trial against sorafenib, and RTOG 1112 also used a sorafenib comparator; neither has been repeated against a modern immunotherapy backbone. {{29543938|39699905}}</p>
  <div class="callout"><b>Document explicitly why local therapy is being added and when systemic therapy starts or resumes.</b> The most common harm in this group is a delayed systemic start, not the radiation itself.</div>
</div>`},

{id:"resp", name:"Response assessment", html:`
<div class="card">
  <h3>Response assessment</h3>
  <p class="kicker">The response-assessment framework is expert consensus, grade C/D — not randomised evidence. v0.2's figure graded this step A; that is corrected.</p>
  <div class="tablewrap"><table><thead><tr><th style="width:16%">Treatment</th><th style="width:16%">First assessment</th><th style="width:30%">Framework</th><th>Mandatory return question</th></tr></thead><tbody>
   <tr><td><b>Ablation or TACE</b></td><td>About 4–6 weeks</td><td>LI-RADS treatment response, <b>nonradiation</b> algorithm v2024; AFP and liver function.</td><td>Complete response? Residual viable target? New untreated disease? Is retreatment safe?</td></tr>
   <tr><td><b>Radioembolisation or SBRT</b></td><td>Usually 8–12 weeks, then serially</td><td>LI-RADS treatment response, <b>radiation</b> algorithm v2024; recognise the nonprogressing category and expect delayed necrosis.</td><td>Is enhancement decreasing or stable, or truly progressing? Is liver function preserved?</td></tr>
   <tr><td><b>Systemic therapy</b></td><td>Every 6–12 weeks by regimen and tempo</td><td>RECIST 1.1 for trials and extrahepatic disease; mRECIST may supplement assessment of intrahepatic viable tumour but should not drive a switch decision alone.</td><td>Continue, manage toxicity, add local control, switch line, or move to symptom-focused care?</td></tr>
   <tr><td><b>Transplant waitlist</b></td><td>At least every 3 months</td><td>Viable tumour burden, AFP and its trajectory, vascular and extrahepatic status, exception status.</td><td>Still within criteria? Bridge or downstage needed? Internal hold? Who owns the next step?</td></tr>
   <tr><td><b>After complete response</b></td><td>Every 3–6 months for two years, then every six months, at least five years</td><td>Multiphase liver CT or MRI, chest imaging as appropriate, AFP with its trend. Care for the underlying liver disease continues alongside.</td><td>New lesion, rising AFP, or change in liver function — back to MDT? Which option now applies?</td></tr>
  </tbody></table></div>
  <p style="margin-top:12px">Every reassessment returns to the MDT when there is viable tumour, discordant interpretation, a new lesion, stage migration, treatment toxicity, a change in transplant eligibility, or uncertainty about the next modality.</p>
</div>`}
];

 ["Exception points follow successful downstaging.",

The initial request and the first extension receive calculated MELD; only an extension after the first receives MMaT-3, and since each exception runs 90 days two periods elapse first, roughly six months. Policy states the score table, not a six-month rule, the rule changes without notice to this document, and no outcome evidence shows that the waiting construct selects better transplant candidates. MMaT is the median MELD at transplant for the donor hospital in that match run, not one national number.",
  "The current Policy 9 text on the day of the decision, the acquisition circle, and local policy where it is stricter.",
  "A named owner and a calendar date for re-verifying Policy 9 criteria against this document; listing dates against first exception request dates."],
 ["Checkpoint inhibitors before transplant are manageable with a washout.",
  "Kayali’s 52-patient pooled review concerns checkpoint inhibitors given after transplantation and cannot define a pre-transplant washout. Pre-LT cohorts provide observational timing evidence. AASLD advises discontinuation at least three months before LT, but no universally safe interval is validated and rejection can still occur. Transplant-specific review must document the interval, prior immune toxicity, alternatives and immunosuppression plan before exposure.",
  "Whether a graft may become available early, the agreed immunosuppression plan, the alternative bridging strategy, and transplant-specific review before the first dose rather than after.",
  "Every pre-transplant checkpoint exposure logged with the agreed washout, the date of the last dose, the date of transplant and the rejection outcome."],
 ["TACE is the standard of care for intermediate-stage HCC, grade A.",
  "The randomised base is two small trials. Llovet 2002 randomised 112 of 903 screened patients (12%) and was stopped at the ninth sequential inspection after 71 deaths against a planned 85 per comparison, giving a hazard ratio of 0.47 (95% CI 0.25 to 0.91) for chemoembolisation versus no anticancer treatment, with the single baseline imbalance, a lower bilirubin in the chemoembolisation arm, adjusted for after it was seen. Its bland embolisation arm achieved a similar response rate without a significant survival benefit (adjusted HR 0.57, 95% CI 0.31 to 1.04). Lo 2002 analysed 79 patients at one Hong Kong centre, relative risk of death 0.50 (0.31 to 0.81), with no benefit demonstrable in tumours over 5 cm or in unilobar portal vein obstruction. The Cochrane review that pooled the randomised embolisation trials found no survival benefit once trials with early stopping and co-interventions were excluded (HR 1.22, 95% CI 0.82 to 1.83) and none in trials at low risk of selection bias (HR 0.88, 0.71 to 1.10). The comparator in both trials was no anticancer treatment, which no longer exists.",
  "Selectivity achievable, portal flow, ALBI and liver-function trajectory, and whether a declared control or downstaging goal exists at all.",
  "Decompensation at 30 and 90 days after TACE; number of sessions per patient and liver-function change across them."],
 ["Drug-eluting-bead and conventional TACE are equivalent.",
  "Equivalence was never shown; superiority failed twice. PRECISION V was a phase 2 trial that missed its primary endpoint, 6-month objective response of 51.6% versus 43.5%, a difference of 8.1% (two-sided 95% repeated confidence interval minus 4.8 to 22.6), one-sided P = 0.11, with no time-to-progression or survival data at all and a fixed 150 mg doxorubicin dose against a body-surface-area-adjusted comparator. PRECISION ITALIA stopped for futility at 177 of a planned 214 patients: 2-year survival 56.8% versus 55.4% (P = 0.949) and median time to progression 9 months in both arms. The one reproducible difference is pain, in 22 of 89 (24.7%) after beads versus 63 of 88 (71.6%) after conventional TACE, with grade 3 pain in 0 versus 16 (18.2%).",
  "Selectivity achieved, operator familiarity, cost, and the pain burden the patient will carry.",
  "Objective response and decompensation by bead versus lipiodol technique, and post-procedural analgesia requirement."],
 ["Radioembolisation is an alternative to TACE in BCLC B.",
  "PREMIERE improved time to progression without a demonstrated survival difference, but 35 of its 45 patients were BCLC A. It stopped for slow accrual at 45 of a planned 124 patients with no prespecified interim analysis, so the hazard ratio of 0.122 rests on 12 progression events with a confidence interval of 0.027 to 0.557, and median overall survival was 17.7 versus 18.6 months (P = 0.99). Half the radioembolisation arm was Child-Pugh B at first treatment versus 24% in the TACE arm. TRACE, a single-centre phase II trial, improved time to progression and overall survival against DEB-TACE (median 30.2 versus 15.6 months, HR 0.48, 95% CI 0.28 to 0.82, whole intention-to-treat population, 85% BCLC B) but was stopped early at interim analysis with 72 of the 136 patients needed, and the TACE arm carried 5 grade 5 events including three definitely treatment-related septic deaths against one after radioembolisation, so the control arm may have been harmed rather than the treatment arm helped. This supports selected disease-control use, not proof of cure or superiority to resection or ablation.",
  "Unilobar versus bilobar distribution, shunt fraction, remnant volume, whether hypertrophy is a goal.",
  "Time to progression, decompensation at 90 days, downstaging rate."],
 ["Radiation segmentectomy is a curative-intent option for ablation-unsuitable solitary tumours.",
  "Single-arm data only, and the endpoints are imaging. RASER treated 29 patients with a solitary tumour of 3 cm or less: target-lesion complete response in 24 of 29 (83%), a sustained complete response after one treatment in 26 of 29 (90%), target-lesion progression in 3 of 29 (10%) and overall progression in 9 of 29 (31%) at a median follow-up of 691 days, read by one unblinded in-house radiologist with no comparator and 5 of 29 (17%) lost to follow-up. All 8 explants showed 100% necrosis of the target lesion, but 3 of those 8 livers held additional untreated HCC, one with vascular invasion. LEGACY is retrospective, 162 patients, median tumour 2.7 cm with 62% under 3 cm: best response of 88.3% (95% CI 82.4 to 92.4) by localised mRECIST falls to a confirmed 46.3% (38.8 to 54.0) by RECIST 1.1, and 45 patients (28%) went on to transplant or resection, so its 86.6% 3-year survival cannot be attributed to the radiation. Both studies were funded by the microsphere manufacturer.",
  "Segmental anatomy, tumour size, remnant volume, dosimetry feasibility, transplant timing.",
  "Complete response, local progression, and transplant explant pathology."],
 ["Lobar radioembolisation grows the contralateral lobe enough to make an unresectable patient resectable.",
  "Radiation lobectomy rests on one retrospective single-centre volumetric cohort of 83 patients, only 67 with HCC, selected post hoc from about 700 lobar treatments with no portal vein embolisation comparator. A future liver remnant above 40% was reached in 25 of 83 (30%), median maximal hypertrophy was 26% (range minus 14 to 86), and the 45% figure required more than 9 months of waiting, during which median Child-Pugh deteriorated from 6 to 7 and new left-lobe tumours appeared in 13 of 67 HCC patients (19%) at a median of 224 days. Only 11 of 83 patients (13%) reached surgery, 5 resections and 6 transplants. The remnant is a volume ratio with irradiated parenchyma in the denominator and no functional test was done, so the gain may overstate the safe remnant.",
  "How long the patient can wait, whether portal vein embolisation would be faster, functional rather than volumetric remnant assessment, and the risk of new contralateral disease during the interval.",
  "Remnant volume and function before and after, interval to operation, and the proportion who actually reach resection."],
 ["Personalised dosimetry is now the standard for radioembolisation.",
  "DOSISPHERE-01 is a phase 2 trial of 60 randomised and 56 treated patients, stopped at a planned interim analysis for efficacy on an unmasked investigator-read endpoint, the EASL response of a single index lesion at 3 months: 20 of 28 (71%) versus 10 of 28 (36%), P = 0.0074. Overall survival of 26.6 versus 10.7 months (HR 0.421, 95% CI 0.215 to 0.826) is a secondary endpoint resting on 14 deaths in the personalised arm, and progression-free survival, the harder endpoint, did not differ (HR 0.71, 0.39 to 1.30, P = 0.26). Ten of 28 patients in the personalised arm went on to curative resection versus one, so part of the survival difference is surgery. Entry required an index lesion of 7 cm or more and 30% hepatic reserve, and the authors state generalisability to lesions under 7 cm and to resin microspheres is untested. The sponsor makes the device.",
  "Index lesion size, hepatic reserve, whether an ablative tumour dose is achievable, and whether conversion to surgery is the actual goal.",
  "Prescribed and achieved tumour absorbed dose recorded for every treatment; response by dose band."],
 ["Radioembolisation is not a substitute for systemic therapy in advanced HCC.",
  "The position is right but the evidence behind it is weaker than it looks. SARAH gave an intention-to-treat overall survival of 8.0 versus 9.9 months (HR 1.15, 95% CI 0.94 to 1.41, P = 0.18) while 53 of 237 patients (22%) assigned radioembolisation never received it; per protocol the medians were identical at 9.9 months (HR 0.99, 0.79 to 1.24). SIRveNIB gave 8.8 versus 10.0 months (HR 1.12, 0.9 to 1.4, P = 0.36) with only 130 of 182 (71.4%) treated, and patients from 5 of its 11 countries flew to Singapore for treatment. SORAMIC was negative in intention to treat (HR 1.01, 0.81 to 1.25) with 47.2% of patients missing the allocated treatment or having major protocol deviations. All three used body-surface-area or manufacturer-recommended activity rather than personalised dosimetry, and SARAH's own dose-response analysis found median survival of 14.1 months when the tumour absorbed dose reached 100 Gy or more versus 6.1 months below it. The comparator in all three was sorafenib, which is no longer first line.",
  "Whether the disease is truly liver-dominant, the delay to the systemic start, dosimetry capability, and liver-function cost.",
  "Time from decision to systemic-therapy start; patients who received a liver-directed procedure instead of a first-line systemic combination."],
 ["SBRT controls HCC better than thermal ablation.",
  "The only randomised comparison enrolled 166 patients with a solitary recurrent HCC of 5 cm or less after curative treatment, and its primary endpoint was a composite local progression-free survival that counts death from any cause: HR 0.45 (95% CI 0.24 to 0.87), P = 0.014, 3-year rate 84.3% versus 67.3%. The arms reached that endpoint differently, 8 of 14 SBRT events being deaths without local progression against 7 of 27 for RFA, so the result turns on 14 local progression events. Progression-free survival (HR 0.76, 0.50 to 1.15, P = 0.190) and overall survival (HR 0.91, 0.37 to 2.22, P = 0.830, 19 deaths) were indistinguishable, and the advantage was significant only in tumours of 2 cm or less (HR 0.39, 0.17 to 0.89), not at 2 to 5 cm (0.58, 0.20 to 1.68, P = 0.310). The retrospective Michigan series pointing the other way, with the SBRT advantage growing with size, had channelled allocation: the SBRT group had a median of 2 prior liver-directed treatments versus 0 and better Child-Pugh. Overall survival was identical there too.",
  "Anatomical suitability for a percutaneous route, tumour size, uninvolved liver volume, prior radiation dose, and whether a bridge to transplant is intended.",
  "Local progression and liver-function change at 12 months by modality; proportion of SBRT cases chosen for anatomy rather than after ablation failure."],
 ["External beam radiotherapy gives survival comparable with resection and ablation in early HCC.",
  "The figures BCLC 2026 cites come from a retrospective individual-patient cohort with no resection, ablation or TACE arm: 4,913 patients from 30 of 96 eligible centres (31%), the centres identified because they had published favourable outcomes. Median overall survival was 6.8 years (95% CI 5.7 to 8.7) for BCLC-0, 4.6 (4.1 to 5.1) for BCLC-A and 3.6 (3.0 to 4.9) for BCLC-B, but 58% of the cohort was BCLC-C, 60% had been treated before, BCLC stage had to be re-adjudicated because reported staging was discordant, and treatment-naive BCLC-B patients survived 6.3 years, longer than treatment-naive BCLC-A, which is not a believable ordering. The proportional hazards assumption was formally violated in all four Cox models and the authors say their hazard ratios should be interpreted with caution. ASTRO's strong recommendation for EBRT as a potential first-line single therapy rests on single-arm and retrospective series; its own task force states no randomised trial has compared EBRT with thermal ablation or catheter-based therapy, and surgical oncologists published a formal dissent.",
  "Whether surgery, transplant or ablation has actually been excluded and why; uninvolved liver volume; prior dose; decompensation risk.",
  "Child-Pugh and ALBI change at 3 and 12 months after liver radiotherapy; proportion of EBRT cases in whom resection or ablation was never formally assessed."],
 ["Adding SBRT or radioembolisation to systemic therapy helps liver-dominant BCLC C.",
  "No randomised test against a modern immunotherapy backbone. RTOG 1112 missed its primary endpoint: median overall survival 15.8 months (90% CI 11.4 to 19.2) versus 12.3 (10.6 to 14.3), HR 0.77 (90% CI 0.59 to 1.01), one-sided P = .06, and significance appears only in the multivariable model (HR 0.72, P = .04). It needed 368 patients and 277 events, closed early in March 2021 and analysed 177 patients and 153 deaths at 65% power; 13 of 85 patients (15%) in the SBRT arm never started sorafenib and 19 of 92 (20.7%) controls later received radiotherapy. The Asan trial of TACE plus 40 Gy against sorafenib reported overall survival of 55.0 versus 43.0 weeks (HR 0.61, 95% CI 0.38 to 0.98) as a secondary endpoint, but 90.7% of the sorafenib arm had crossed over by 24 weeks, so it compares two sequencing strategies, and it never reported how many of its 90 patients had cirrhosis. The neoadjuvant radiotherapy trial for portal vein tumour thrombus that ASTRO cites counted only tumour-related death, drew 157 of 164 patients from one hospital and cost 11% of patients their operation.",
  "Liver-dominant burden, symptom burden, uninvolved-liver volume, prior dose, time to systemic start.",
  "Time from decision to systemic-therapy start; hepatic progression-free survival."],
 ["SBRT is a reasonable option for residual disease after an incomplete TACE.",
  "One randomised trial of 40 patients at a single Italian centre supports it, against a planned 50, powered on an implausible hazard ratio of 0.18. One-year local control was 84% versus 23% (HR 0.15, 95% CI 0.04 to 0.4, P = 0.0002) and progression-free survival 9 versus 4 months (HR 0.43, 0.21 to 0.87), but distant recurrence-free survival did not differ and overall survival was identical at 31 versus 30 months (P = 0.472). The comparator was mostly bland embolisation, 15 of 19, not conventional or drug-eluting-bead TACE, and 10 of 19 control patients crossed over to SBRT. The parallel randomised comparison of SBRT with DEB-TACE as primary therapy, TRENDY, closed at 30 of 100 planned patients and was negative on its primary endpoint (time to progression HR 0.45, 95% CI 0.16 to 1.32, P = .15); its quoted 100% versus 54% local control is a post hoc per-protocol analysis, the prespecified comparison giving P = .075.",
  "Whether a viable target remains and is reachable, liver-function trajectory, prior dose to that volume, and what a well-selected TACE rechallenge would achieve.",
  "Local control and decompensation after consolidative SBRT; cases re-embolised versus irradiated after an incomplete first TACE."],
 ["Histotripsy met its endpoints in the HOPE4LIVER pivotal trial.",
  "It met a technical endpoint in a population that is not the one a tumour board would send for ablation. The co-primary endpoints were technical success, 42 of 44 treated tumours (95%, 95% CI 84 to 100) against a 70% performance goal that the authors say was agreed with the FDA for achievable enrolment and was not intended to identify a difference from existing therapies, and procedure-related major complications, 3 of 44 participants (7%, 2 to 18) against a 25% goal. Neither is tumour control. Only 18 of 44 participants (41%) had HCC, 4 of the 25 metastatic patients had more than 20 liver lesions, mean tumour diameter was 1.5 cm, the treatment zone averaged 3.6 cm, 38 of 44 tumours were in segments II to IV and none in segments VII or VIII. Technique efficacy had already fallen to 83% (30 of 36) at 30 days, and one grade 5 hepatic failure occurred in 44 participants despite the planned volume being achieved. The one-year update of 47 patients and 52 tumours reports freedom from local progression of 63.4% on the prespecified core-laboratory read against 90% on a post hoc read made once all imaging was available, with reader agreement of 70.8% to 84%; 12-month overall survival was 58.6% overall and 73.3% in HCC. FDA clearance for tumour destruction is a safety and performance determination.",
  "Acoustic window and target visibility, segment, device working range, and whether any established curative option would be displaced.",
  "Every histotripsy case in a prospective registry with the prespecified rather than post hoc local-control read; one-year local progression and liver-function change."],
 ["Three first-line immunotherapy combinations are interchangeable because none is ranked above the others.",
  "None has been compared with another, and each was tested against a different and now-superseded comparator, so the absence of a ranking is a gap, not a finding. IMbrave150 gave 19.2 versus 13.4 months against sorafenib (HR 0.66, 95% CI 0.52 to 0.85) but its exploratory non-viral subgroup was imprecise (HR for death 1.05, 95% CI 0.68 to 1.63; median 17.0 versus 18.1 months), without proof of no benefit or a validated treatment-selection interaction, and only 422 of 1,447 real-world patients on tyrosine-kinase inhibitors (29%) would have met its eligibility. HIMALAYA gave 16.43 versus 13.77 months (HR 0.78, 96.02% CI 0.65 to 0.93) with no progression-free survival benefit at all (HR 0.90, 0.77 to 1.05), curves separating only after 9 months, and main portal vein thrombosis excluded. CheckMate 9DW gave 23.7 versus 20.6 months against lenvatinib or sorafenib (HR 0.79, 0.65 to 0.96) with crossing hazards, a piecewise hazard ratio of 1.65 (1.12 to 2.43) in the first 6 months, 12 treatment-related deaths against 3 with 11 of the 12 inside that window and 9 of them fatal hepatic events, a restricted mean survival difference of only 2.8 months (0.2 to 5.4) at 47 months, and Vp4 invasion excluded.",
  "Variceal and bleeding risk, aetiology, how much runway the patient has in the first six months, autoimmune history, and transplant intent.",
  "Early mortality at 6 months by regimen; variceal assessment documented before the first dose of atezolizumab-bevacizumab."],
 ["There is a second-line sequence after a first-line immunotherapy combination.",
  "There is no randomised evidence for any sequence after a modern combination; every agent on the list was tested after sorafenib, in a population that no longer exists, and each gain is small. CELESTIAL gave 10.2 versus 8.0 months (HR 0.76, 95% CI 0.63 to 0.92) but stopped at 484 of 621 planned deaths (78%), with a hazard ratio of 1.11 in hepatitis C disease, grade 3 or 4 events in 68% and a median delivered dose of 35.8 mg against an intended 60. RESORCE gave 10.6 versus 7.8 months (HR 0.63, 0.50 to 0.79) but enrolled only patients who had tolerated sorafenib at 400 mg or more, and every treated patient had an adverse event. REACH-2 gave 8.5 versus 7.3 months (HR 0.710, 0.531 to 0.949) with no significant response (5% versus 1%) and no improvement in symptoms, and its baseline AFP was imbalanced against the experimental arm, so adjusting for it dropped the placebo median to 6.7 months. KEYNOTE-394 gave 14.6 versus 13.0 months at a one-sided P of .0180 against a boundary of .0193, with 85% of patients from mainland China and about 80% hepatitis B.",
  "Prior toxicity, best response achieved, liver function now, AFP for the ramucirumab indication, and trial availability first.",
  "Reason for selection recorded for every second-line decision; grade 3 or higher toxicity and liver-function change by agent."],
 ["TACE combined with checkpoint inhibitors is to be avoided outside a protocol.",
  "The position is correct, but it rests on absent survival benefit rather than on demonstrated harm, and the toxicity is the measured part. All three phase 3 trials met a progression-free survival endpoint and none has shown an overall-survival benefit. EMERALD-1 gave 15.0 versus 8.2 months (HR 0.77, 95% CI 0.61 to 0.98, P = 0.032) with durvalumab plus TACE no better than TACE alone (HR 0.94, 0.75 to 1.19), so the effect appears to come from bevacizumab with no bevacizumab-plus-TACE arm to confirm it, and its interim survival analysis was withheld. LEAP-012 gave 14.6 versus 10.0 months (HR 0.66, 0.51 to 0.84) with an interim overall-survival hazard ratio of 0.80 (0.57 to 1.11, one-sided P = 0.087 against a 0.0012 threshold) and a final registry-posted figure of 0.98; its progression definition required new intrahepatic tumours to meet LI-RADS 5 criteria, and without that rule the placebo median fell from 10.0 to 8.4 months. EMERALD-3 gave 13.0 versus 9.8 months (HR 0.70, 0.57 to 0.86) with overall survival at 40% maturity of 39.5 versus 34.7 months (HR 0.84, 0.65 to 1.09, P = 0.18) and a restricted mean survival difference of 1.48 months (minus 1.21 to 4.16). The cost is grade 3 or worse treatment-related events in 71% versus 32% in LEAP-012 and 63% versus 19% in EMERALD-3, immune-mediated events in 48%, and treatment-related deaths in 4 and 7 patients. Over 40% of each trial was outside BCLC B and none had a TACE-free arm, so the question of whether to add TACE to systemic therapy rather than the reverse is untouched.",
  "Tumour burden and stage, liver function, performance status, variceal status, goals of therapy, and whether the same drugs given sequentially after progression would do as well.",
  "Every protocol or registry case logged with its selection rationale, grade 3 or higher toxicity and liver-function trajectory."],
 ["There is no adjuvant strategy after resection or ablation.",
  "That statement concerns atezolizumab plus bevacizumab in a global population, and it is correct for that question: IMbrave050 was declared positive at a first interim analysis under stopping rules assuming proportional hazards that did not hold, recurrence-free survival hazard ratio 0.72 (adjusted 95% CI 0.53 to 0.98), and the updated analysis lost it, median 33.2 versus 36.0 months, HR 0.90 (0.72 to 1.12), with overall survival numerically unfavourable (HR 1.26, 0.85 to 1.87) on 100 deaths among 668 patients, 30% crossover, grade 3 or 4 events in 36% to 41% versus 13% and grade 5 events in 6 patients (2%) versus 1. It is not a statement about every adjuvant strategy. Two Chinese randomised trials report benefit and the page is silent on them: one cycle of reduced-dose adjuvant TACE after resection of high-risk HBV-related HCC gave 3-year recurrence-free survival of 56.0% versus 42.1% (HR 0.68, 95% CI 0.49 to 0.93) and overall survival of 85.2% versus 77.4% (HR 0.59, 0.36 to 0.97) on 64 deaths, in 280 of 1,393 consecutive resections at one centre with an unblinded surveillance control that never had the extra angiogram; adjuvant FOLFOX hepatic arterial infusion for microvascular invasion gave median disease-free survival of 20.3 versus 10.0 months (HR 0.59, 0.43 to 0.81) with overall survival not significant (HR 0.64, 0.36 to 1.14) on 47 deaths, and microvascular invasion was neither graded nor used for stratification.",
  "Whether the patient resembles the trial populations at all, the recurrence risk recorded at resection, surveillance intensity, and trial availability.",
  "Recurrence detected on surveillance and the proportion salvaged with curative intent; any adjuvant therapy given outside a trial, with its rationale."],
 ["Hepatic arterial infusion is trial-only because the evidence is immature.",
  "The randomised evidence is not immature; it is geographically narrow and partly a conversion-surgery effect. FOHAIC-1 gave median overall survival of 13.9 versus 8.2 months against sorafenib (HR 0.408, 95% CI 0.301 to 0.552) at a single Chinese centre, 92% hepatitis B, median tumour 11.2 cm. Against conventional TACE in large HCC, FOLFOX infusion gave 23.1 versus 16.1 months (HR 0.58, 0.45 to 0.75), but 24% of that arm went on to curative resection versus 12%, and the authors concede the gap would be narrower without prompt resection. Added to sorafenib in portal vein invasion it gave 13.37 versus 7.13 months (HR 0.35, 0.26 to 0.48), with 16 of 125 patients resected versus 1. Every trial is Chinese, open-label, predominantly hepatitis B, and the comparators are sorafenib or conventional TACE; the technique needed a median of 2 catheter-tip repositionings per cycle and collateral re-embolisation in 54% of patients, and the investigators argue this is why it succeeded where implanted-port trials failed.",
  "Whether a conversion-to-surgery goal is declared and realistic, interventional capacity for repeated catheterisation, and whether a first-line systemic combination is being displaced.",
  "Every HAIC case with a named goal, the number of cycles delivered, and whether resection followed."],
 ["A fixed two-session TACE failure threshold is not a universal rule.",
  "A pragmatic consensus threshold, not a validated rule; published TACE-refractoriness definitions differ. EASL states that after one or two consecutive TACEs without response other therapies should be considered, at level of evidence 3, and no study has compared switching at a fixed session count with reassessing after each session. v0.8 withdrew the fixed rule in favour of reassessment after each session.",
  "Selectivity achieved, response pattern, liver-function trajectory, remaining downstaging goal.",
  "Outcomes of patients switched at two sessions versus continued."],
 ["Bridging therapy on the waiting list reduces dropout, and the modality does not matter.",
  "The Toronto comparative series is a single-centre retrospective intention-to-treat analysis in which the arms were not comparable and SBRT was by design reserved for patients who could not have TACE or RFA. Dropout was 6 of 36 (16.7%) after SBRT, 20 of 99 (20.2%) after TACE and 41 of 244 (16.8%) after RFA (P = 0.7), but only 13 of 36 SBRT patients (36.1%) and 22 of 99 TACE patients (22.7%) were within Milan against 214 of 244 RFA patients (87.7%), and the SBRT arm had higher MELD and worse Child-Pugh. Explant complete necrosis was 4 of 30 (13.3%) after SBRT versus 17 of 70 (24.3%) after TACE and 87 of 177 (49.2%) after RFA (P below 0.001), and liver function deteriorated after SBRT in 38.9% versus 19.4% and 13.0%. With 6 dropouts in the SBRT arm the study is underpowered for its own endpoint and the authors read it as feasibility, not equivalence. No trial has compared bridging with no bridging.",
  "Expected waiting time, liver function, whether the tumour is the threat to listing or the cirrhosis is, and what the explant is likely to show.",
  "Waitlist dropout and explant necrosis by bridging modality; number of locoregional procedures before transplant."],
 ["An approximate 10 to 12 case agenda cap improves decision quality.",
  "An operational judgement with no comparative outcome evidence. The same applies to the quality targets on this page: the 90% and 95% thresholds, the one-business-day urgent triage standard and the three-procedure investigation trigger are all chosen rather than derived, and the curative-first discipline measure is new and was previously unmeasured.",
  "Case complexity mix, attendance, available time, urgent-lane volume.",
  "Decision completeness and deferral rate by agenda length."]
];

/* ---------- helpers ---------- */
const esc = s => String(s).replace(/[&<>"]/g, c => ({"&":"&","<":"<",">":">",'"':"""}[c]));
function refTag(id){ const r = REF[id] || NONPM[id]; return r ? r[0] : id; }
function refChips(ids){
  if(!ids || !ids.length) return "";
  return '<div class="refs">' + ids.map(id =>
    `<button class="refchip" data-ref="${id}" type="button">${esc(refTag(id))}</button>`).join("") + '</div>';
}
/* {{pmid|pmid}} inline markers become chips */
function expand(html){
  return html.replace(/\{\{([^}]+)\}\}/g, (m, ids) => refChips(ids.split("|")));
}

/* ---------- build stage buttons + answer ---------- */
const stageBtns = document.getElementById("stageBtns");
stageBtns.innerHTML = STAGES.map(s => `
  <button class="st" type="button" data-stage="${s.id}" data-tone="${s.tone}" aria-pressed="false">
    <span class="sname">${esc(s.name)}</span>
    <span class="sreq">${reqLabel(s.req)}</span>
    <ul class="scrit">${s.crit.map(c => `<li>${esc(c)}</li>`).join("")}</ul>
  </button>`).join("");

/* Collapsed by default: the stage reads as a list of options at rest, and the
   criteria, cautions and sources open on demand. */
function detail(o){
  const bits = [];
  if(o.pref)  bits.push(`<div class="optline"><span class="optlab">Preferred when</span><span>${esc(o.pref)}</span></div>`);
  if(o.avoid) bits.push(`<div class="optline bad"><span class="optlab">Caution / avoid</span><span>${esc(o.avoid)}</span></div>`);
  if(o.note)  bits.push(`<div class="recnote" style="margin-top:7px">${esc(o.note)}</div>`);
  const chips = refChips(o.refs);
  if(chips) bits.push(`<div style="margin-top:8px">${chips}</div>`);
  if(!bits.length) return "";
  const n = (o.refs||[]).length;
  const label = [o.pref||o.avoid ? "Criteria and cautions" : "", n ? n + (n===1?" source":" sources") : ""]
                .filter(Boolean).join(" · ");
  return `<details class="more"><summary>${esc(label)}</summary><div class="moreinner">${bits.join("")}</div></details>`;
}
function recHTML(r){
  const cls = LABELCLS[r.l] || "p-std";
  const flags = (r.flags||[]).map(f=>`<span class="flag">${esc(f)}</span>`).join(" ");
  const body = r.opts ? `
    <div class="opts">${r.opts.map((o,i)=>`
      <div class="opt">
        <div class="optn">${r.rank === false ? "·" : i+1}</div>
        <div style="min-width:0">
          <div class="optname">${esc(o.name)}${o.g?`<span class="grade ${o.g}">${o.g}</span>`:""}${(o.flags||[]).map(f=>`<span class="flag">${esc(f)}</span>`).join(" ")}</div>
          <div class="optwhen">${esc(o.when)}</div>
          ${detail(o)}
        </div>
      </div>`).join("")}</div>

  const c = MX.cells[mCell];
  const mod = MX.modalities.find(x=>x[0]===mCell.split("|")[1]);
  document.querySelectorAll(".mcell").forEach(b=>b.setAttribute("aria-pressed", String(b.dataset.cell===mCell)));
  document.getElementById("lrtDetail").innerHTML = `
    <div class="ahead" style="padding:0 0 12px; border-bottom:1px solid var(--line2)">
      <h3 style="font-size:20px">${esc(mod[1])} <span class="muted" style="font-family:var(--sans); font-weight:400">in hepatocellular carcinoma</span></h3>
      ${tchip(c.tier, MX.tiers[c.tier].label)}
    </div>
    <p style="margin-top:12px; font-size:14.5px"><b>${esc(expandAbbr(c.head))}</b></p>
    ${c.roles.map(r=>`<div class="role">
        <div class="rolewhen">${tchip(r.t, (MX.tiers[r.t] || {short:"Caution"}).short)}<span>${esc(expandAbbr(r.when))}</span></div>
        <details class="more"><summary>${r.ev.length} ${r.ev.length===1?"trial":"trials"}</summary>
          <div class="moreinner">${r.ev.map(evLine).join("")}</div></details>
      </div>`).join("")}`;
  const ci = MX.contra && MX.contra[mod[0]];
  if(ci) document.getElementById("lrtDetail").innerHTML += `<div class="role" style="border-top:1px solid var(--line2);margin-top:16px;padding-top:12px"><h4>Contraindications and feasibility</h4><ul>${ci.items.map(x=>`<li>${esc(x)}</li>`).join("")}</ul><p class="small muted">${esc(ci.ref.join(" · "))}</p></div>`;

}
document.getElementById("mcards").addEventListener("click", e=>{
  const b = e.target.closest(".mcell"); if(!b) return;
  mCell = b.dataset.cell;
  renderCell();
});

/* the critique store loads on its own and re-renders the library when it lands,
   so a missing or slow file never holds up the rest of the page */
fetch("data/critique.json?v=20261023-language").then(r=>r.ok?r.json():{}).catch(()=>({}))
  .then(c=>{ CRIT = c || {}; renderEv(); });

Promise.all([
  fetch("../lrt/matrix.json?v=20261102-review1").then(r=>r.json()),
  fetch("data/lrt_refs.json?v=20261027-depot").then(r=>r.json())
]).then(([mx, refs])=>{
  MX = mx;
  renderTierLegend(); renderCards(); renderCell();
  // only the papers this tumour's cells actually cite go into the library
  const used = new Set(["39962001", "36346892", "24154839"]);
  for(const [key, c] of Object.entries(MX.cells)){
    if(!key.startsWith(TUM+"|")) continue;
    for(const role of c.roles) for(const e of role.ev) if(e[1]) used.add(e[1]);
  }
  const have = new Set(ALL.map(r=>r.id));
  for(const r of refs){
    if(have.has(r.pmid) || !used.has(r.pmid)) continue;
    ALL.push({id:r.pmid, tag:(r.au||"")+" "+(r.y||""), group:"Liver-directed",
              cit:`${r.au} et al. ${r.t} ${r.j}. ${r.y}.`.replace(/\s+/g," "),
              pmid:r.pmid, depot:r.st==="depot"});
    have.add(r.pmid);
  }
  RoadmapEvidence.merge(ALL);
  const groups = [...new Set(ALL.map(r=>r.group))];
  document.getElementById("evGroups").innerHTML = ["All",...groups].map((g,i)=>
    `<button class="tab" type="button" data-group="${esc(g)}" aria-selected="${String(g===evGroup)}">${esc(g)}</button>`).join("");
  renderEv();
}).catch(err=>{
  document.getElementById("lrtDetail").innerHTML =
    `<p class="muted">The matrix data did not load. The rest of the page is unaffected; reload to try again.</p>`;
  document.getElementById("tierLegend").innerHTML = "";
});

/* ---------- reference chips jump to the library ---------- */
document.addEventListener("click", e=>{
  const c = e.target.closest(".refchip"); if(!c) return;
  const id = c.dataset.ref;
  setFold("evBody", true);          // the library is folded by default
  evGroup = "All"; evQuery = "";
  document.getElementById("evSearch").value = "";
  document.querySelectorAll("#evGroups .tab").forEach((x,i)=>x.setAttribute("aria-selected", String(i===0)));
  renderEv();
  const el = document.getElementById("ev-"+id)?.closest(".ev");
  if(el){
    el.scrollIntoView({behavior:"smooth", block:"center"});
    document.querySelectorAll(".ev.hit").forEach(x=>x.classList.remove("hit"));
    el.classList.add("hit");
  }
});
</script>

<script>
/* served as a site rather than a single artifact: give every page the way back */
(function(){
  var nav = document.querySelector("nav.sec");
  if(!nav) return;
  var a = document.createElement("a");
  a.href = "../"; a.textContent = "\u2190 All pathways";
  nav.insertBefore(a, nav.firstChild);
})();

window.addEventListener('hashchange', () => {
  let id; try { id = decodeURIComponent(location.hash.slice(1)); } catch { return; }
  if (!ALL.some(r => id === 'ev-' + r.id || (r.aliases || []).some(a => id === a || id === 'ev-' + a))) return;
  evGroup = 'All'; evQuery = ''; document.getElementById('evSearch').value = '';
  document.querySelectorAll('#evGroups .tab').forEach(b => b.setAttribute('aria-selected', String(b.dataset.group === 'All')));
  renderEv();
});
</script>
</body>
</html>
